name: David Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a digital reporter at the regional TV station's news website, which mostly means I turn the evening bulletin into short videos and web stories, and sometimes go out with a phone and a microphone to shoot my own. I use AI tools all day: subtitles, cutting clips, rough first drafts of web copy that I then fix. I love going out on a story with just my phone. The bit that wears me out is the late shift, cutting the same flood clip into four shapes for four apps.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single, and I rent a small studio flat above a phone repair shop. The pay's on the low side for the job, and the rent takes nearly half. I've got under a month saved, partly because I bought a decent microphone and a gimbal, a stand that keeps the phone steady, on a credit card.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you rate yourself at the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I'm fast with the tools and still learning the journalism. My producer, Nadia, sends back half my scripts because I bury the main point. I'm working on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told people it was mostly a good set of tools, and it is. Online I'd post something like, the tools were never the story, the stories were the story. I'd try to make it funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me, because I'm already squeezing every drop out of the tools that exist. The job doesn't change much. The money's still tight, and the station has been talking about sharing a newsroom with the one in the next region.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and focus on getting better at writing, so Nadia stops sending things back. I'd do more paid video for local businesses at weekends, maybe two jobs a month, to pay off the credit card. I'd keep an eye on that shared-newsroom plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly relaxed, with the money worry humming in the back. AI stalling is fine for me, because my problem was never the tools, my problem is the credit card I used to buy a microphone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of business videos?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Short promo clips for the bike shop, a café, a garage. Fifty-second things for their social pages. I charge about a hundred and fifty each, which is cheap, but it adds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shared newsroom mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer digital reporters, probably. If they merge, there might be one web desk for both regions. I'd need to be the faster, better one.

say: I'd say AI was always a **good set of tools**, nothing more.
I'd post that **the stories** were always the real story.
think: The plateau is **fine for me**, since I already use the tools fully.
The real worries are **tight money** and a possible **shared newsroom**.
do: Focus on **writing better scripts** so Nadia stops sending them back.
Shoot **two business videos** a month to clear the credit card.
feel: Fairly **relaxed**, with a **money worry** humming underneath.
S0.quote: AI stalling is fine for me, because my problem was never the tools, my problem is the credit card I used to buy a microphone.
fieldNote: He's comfortable with tools and sees **writing** as his real weakness.
A **credit card** for kit shows a willingness to take small risks.
A **newsroom merger** worries him more than AI does.

steps.text: Rewrite scripts with Nadia's notes until fewer get sent back
Shoot two paid promo videos a month for local businesses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where people like me should help newsrooms do it well, not badly. At work I'd volunteer to test new tools. Online I'd share what works and what's rubbish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of my current job disappears, the clipping and the web rewrites. The AI will do the four-apps thing on its own. What's left is going out and finding stories, which is the bit I'm worst at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the station to let me run the AI workflow on the web desk, so I'm the one who sets it up. I'd spend saved time going out on stories. And I'd build the business video side, because local firms will want help with this too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit excited. I can see a way through, but I'm not sure I'm good enough to take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bit you're worst at is the bit that's left. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go out more, even on my days off, and pitch my own stories. Nadia says the best web reporters bring in one story a week nobody else has. Software can cut the clip, but software doesn't know the farmer whose field flooded, and I have to be the one who does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older video editor, Kwame, who's brilliant but won't touch the tools. He's going to be asked why it takes him an hour when the software does it in two minutes.

say: I'd say people who know the tools should help newsrooms **do it well**.
I'd volunteer to **test new tools** and share what works online.
think: The **clipping and rewrites** in my job would mostly disappear.
What's left is **finding stories**, the bit I'm worst at.
do: Ask to run the **AI workflow** on the web desk.
Go out on **my own stories**, even on days off.
Grow **business video** work as local firms want help.
feel: **Anxious and excited**, unsure he's good enough.
S1.quote: Software can cut the clip, but software doesn't know the farmer whose field flooded, and I have to be the one who does.
fieldNote: He's honest that his **weak skill** is the one that survives.
His adaptability shows in **volunteering** to own the rollout.
He worries for **Kwame**, an older editor who won't use the tools.

steps.text: Volunteer to set up the AI workflow on the web desk
Pitch one original story a week found on his days off
Offer AI-assisted video packages to local businesses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and nobody's ready, and I'd say we need a proper safety net fast. At work I'd be honest that my job is gone. Online I'd try to explain it calmly to people who don't follow tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be out by 2028 or 2029. My whole job is screen work, the exact thing the card says goes first. My tool skills stop mattering when the tools don't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next two years saving hard and paying off the credit card. I'd look at live event filming and camera work, weddings, sports, things where someone has to be there with a camera, because robots come later. And I'd consider moving to the city, where there's more of that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years means I'd be clearing my credit card just in time to lose the job it was supposed to help me keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come about three years after the thinking AI. How does that play into the camera work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holding a camera at a wedding is hands-on, so it lasts maybe till 2031. Editing it isn't, so that goes in 2028. I'd be selling the being-there part, not the editing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat, maybe. I'd look for a room in a shared house to cut the rent in half, and sell the second lens I barely use.

say: I'd say this is **huge**, nobody's ready, and we need a **safety net**.
I'd try to explain it **calmly** to people who don't follow tech.
think: My job is all **screen work**, so I'd be out by 2028 or 2029.
My **tool skills** stop mattering when the tools don't need me.
do: Pay off the **credit card** and save hard for two years.
Move into **live event filming**, where someone must be there.
Consider moving to the **city** and into a shared house.
S2.quote: Two years means I'd be clearing my credit card just in time to lose the job it was supposed to help me keep.
fieldNote: He splits his own work into **being there** and editing, and sells the first.
The **robot delay** gives him about three years of camera work.
Cutting **rent** comes first in his money plan.

steps.text: Pay off the credit card and save for two years
Start filming weddings and local sports events for pay
Move to a shared house in the city for cheaper rent and more work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan. I'd want the station to be honest with staff. Online I'd share how I'm preparing, in case it helps someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is decent for me. I'd get maybe three more years at the station, learn the reporting side, and save. Then I'd move to something hands-on or face-to-face before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every new tool as it comes, because that keeps me useful longest. I'd build the business video side into a small company with a proper website by year two. I'd take a short course in live broadcast camera operating, the sort used at football matches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. Five years is enough to build a small video business if I stop spending my weekends recovering from late shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of that plan is the hardest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekends. Late shifts wreck me, and I lose Saturdays sleeping. I'd have to ask Nadia to put me on days, which means less overtime pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's just what happens with new technology. Maybe governments for not planning, but I'm not angry at the tools.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan**, so we should plan.
I'd share **how I'm preparing** online in case it helps others.
think: Five years gives me about **three more years** at the station.
I'd move into **hands-on or face-to-face** work before 2031.
do: Learn **every new tool** to stay useful longest.
Turn business videos into a **small company** with a website by year two.
Take a course in **live broadcast camera** operating.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to build a small video business if I stop spending my weekends recovering from late shifts.
fieldNote: He's **practical** and blames no one, true to a centre outlook.
His obstacle is **energy**, not money: late shifts eat his weekends.
He'd trade **overtime pay** for day shifts to build the business.

steps.text: Learn each new newsroom AI tool as it is released
Register the business video work as a small company by year two
Take a short course in live broadcast camera operating

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time, and people like me can do well if we're smart. I'd encourage colleagues to start learning now, gently.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is good for me. I could become a proper reporter, then a producer, and still have time to switch to live camera work before the robots. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and learn the reporting side properly. I'd put money into better camera kit gradually, paid from the business side, not the credit card. And I'd stay on top of the tools, so I'm always the one who knows what's new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with some worry about money. With ten years I'd have time to stop being the kid who's good with apps and become someone who's good at news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay. Ten years on a low wage doesn't build savings. If the station merges with the next region, I could still lose the job before AGI even comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ideally running live camera crews for events, or a small video company. Somewhere I'm in the room.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** for people who plan.
I'd **gently encourage** colleagues to start learning now.
think: Ten years lets me become a **proper reporter**, then a producer.
I'd still switch to **live camera work** before the robots come.
do: Learn the **reporting side** properly at the station.
Buy better **camera kit** slowly, paid from business earnings.
Stay the one who knows the **newest tools**.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd have time to stop being the kid who's good with apps and become someone who's good at news.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **grow in journalism** before switching.
A station **merger** still threatens him before AGI arrives.
He'd fund kit from **business earnings**, a lesson from the credit card.

steps.text: Take on more original reporting shifts at the station
Buy better camera kit with business video earnings
Test each new AI editing tool in the first month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. All my skills are screen skills, and two years isn't long enough to switch with no savings. What would help is short, paid courses in hands-on work, and help getting small video businesses started.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what young people in news are told. Everyone told me to learn the tools so I'd be safe, and nobody told me the tools were learning my job at the same time.

headlineQuote: Everyone told me to learn the tools so I'd be safe, and nobody told me the tools were learning my job at the same time.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old** digital reporter at a regional TV station's website.
He uses **AI tools all day**, rents a small studio, and owes money on a credit card.
He's fast with tools but still **learning journalism**, and admits the human side is his weak spot.
In AGI scenarios he plans to sell **being there** with a camera, using the robot delay.
He blames no one and builds a **side video business** as his main safety net.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because all his skills are screen skills.
